---
title: "Quiz: energy and probability"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Spins $s_p = \pm 1$, energy $E(\mathbf s) = -J\sum_{(p,q)} s_ps_q - h\sum_p s_p$, Gibbs distribution $p(\mathbf s) = e^{-E(\mathbf s)/T}/Z$.

---

**Q1.** Two images differ only in one pixel. The first has energy 3 units lower. At $T = 1$, how much more probable is it? Do you need $Z$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Take the ratio of the two probabilities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$e^{3} \approx 20$ times more probable. $Z$ cancels in the ratio: only the energy difference is needed.
:::

---

**Q2.** What happens to the Gibbs distribution as $T \to 0$? As $T \to \infty$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $e^{-E/T}$ for two different energies when $T$ is tiny, and when it is huge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
As $T \to 0$, all probability goes to the lowest-energy states (the ground states): sampling becomes energy minimisation. As $T \to \infty$, $e^{-E/T} \to 1$ for every state, so all states become equally likely and the energy no longer matters.
:::

---

**Q3.** In a $2 \times 2$ lattice with $J = 1$, $h = 0$, how many states have energy 0, and why can the level $E = 0$ be more probable than the level $E = -4$ although each of its states is less probable?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A level's probability is (number of states) $\times$ (probability of one state).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
12 states: all except the 2 aligned states and the 2 checkerboards. The level has 12 states against 2, so at high enough $T$ (e.g. $T = 4$: 0.66 against 0.30) the many slightly worse states together outweigh the two best ones.
:::

---

**Q4.** What does a positive field $h$ do to the two ground states "all $+1$" and "all $-1$"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Without a field the two have the same energy.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It lowers the energy of "all $+1$" by $nh$ and raises that of "all $-1$" by $nh$. Their probability ratio becomes $e^{2nh/T}$: the field breaks the tie, and "all $+1$" becomes the single most probable state. In an image model the field is the data term.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why can we not compute the probability of one particular $256 \times 256$ binary image under an Ising model?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is needed besides $e^{-E/T}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
We need $Z$, a sum over all $2^{65536} \approx 10^{19728}$ states. It cannot be computed by listing, and in 2D there is no general shortcut. Energies and ratios of probabilities are easy; absolute probabilities are not.
:::

---

**Q6.** For pixels on a line, $Z$ can be computed quickly. What is the trick, and which algorithm from the graph-cut day does it resemble?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Go along the line one pixel at a time.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sum from left to right, keeping the total weight of all partial chains that end in $+1$ and in $-1$; each new pixel updates these two numbers with a $2 \times 2$ table (the transfer matrix). It is dynamic programming on a chain, as in `segchain`, with "minimum" replaced by "sum": $n$ steps instead of $2^n$ terms.
:::

---

**Q7.** On the graph-cut day the smoothness weight was $\lambda$. Which Ising parameter is it, and what plays the role of the data term?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write $s_p = 2L_p - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\lambda = 2J$: a disagreeing pair costs $2J$ more than an agreeing one. The field is the data term: $D_p(1) - D_p(0) = -2h_p$, with a pixel-dependent field $h_p$ when the data differ between pixels. The minimum cut is the Ising ground state.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that $p \propto e^{-E/T}$ is unchanged when a constant is added to every energy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$e^{-(E + c)/T} = e^{-c/T}\,e^{-E/T}$. The factor $e^{-c/T}$ is the same for every state, so it multiplies $Z$ too and cancels in $e^{-(E + c)/T}/Z'$. Only energy differences matter.
:::
